newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Campaign violence spreads in Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: Campaign violence spreads in Indonesia.

text.p: A riot broke out in central Java on Tuesday and troops fired shots into the air in Jakarta as thousands of people poured onto the streets in support of a minority Moslem-backed party contesting May 29 elections.

Witnesses said up to ten thousand supporters of the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) attacked an office of the ruling Golkar party in the town of Pekalongan, about 260 miles (415 km) east of Jakarta.
They said the office, which belongs to the youth wing of Golkar, party, was pelted with stones and ransacked before police fired warning shots and tear gas and dispersed the mob.

Four motorcycles and many Golkar flags were burnt by the crowd and two houses near the Golkar office were damaged, they said. Five people were injured in the violence and about a score were held by police, they said.
In Jakarta, a riot nearly broke out in the Otista area in the east of the city after police earlier broke up a street battle between backers of the PPP and Golkar.
PPP backers also poured into the streets in other heavily-Moslem areas in southern, eastern and central districts of the capital of 10 million people.

Witnesses said police fired tear gas and shots into the air in Otista and other areas but the situation subsequently calmed as peels of thunder rolled across the city and heavy late monsoon rain began to fall.

Some witnesses reported seeing a man in plain clothes firing several shots from a pistol in the direction of demonstrators, but it was not clear if he was using live ammunition and there were no reports of casualties.
The only casualty seen by a Reuters correspondent was a man who was hit in the leg by a teargas cannister. Police took him to hospital in a civilian car.
Diplomats and political analysts said the security force appeared to be careful to avoid firing on the crowds.
In financial markets, the rupiah softened slightly on reports of the violence, easing about three points from the opening to 2,444 against the dollar.
The stock market ended flat, easing back from earlier gains. But the index still closed up 0.28 points at 652.83 points.
The violence flared despite a decision by PPP leaders not to campaign in Jakarta on Tuesday after street battles between its supporters and Golkar rivals last weekend.

The leaders of the PPP, Golkar and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) said on Sunday night they were calling off mass rallies until the end of the election campaign on Friday to avert further violence.

The three parties are the only groups legally entitled to contest the elections for 425 elected seats in the 500-member House of Representatives. The other 75 seats are alloted to the military which does not vote.

The main campaign violence has been in central and west Java between backers of the PPP and Golkar, which is expected to win the election comfortably. There is a five-day cooling off period between the end of the campaign and the actual poll.
Analysts said the PPP hoped to do well in the Jakarta area, but the violence could be counter-productive.
"A lot of the PPP are very young, and they are frightening people who might otherwise be sympathetic to the party," one diplomat said.

Before the campaign, leaders of the three parties had agreed to campaign in separate areas each day to avoid controntations. Tuesday was the PPP's campaign day on Java, the country's most crowded island with 60 percent of Indonesia's 200 million people.
Golkar is seeking to push its share of the vote to more than 70 percent from the 68 percent it won in the last elections in 1992. The PPP then received 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent.
